title: B-epsilon Tree Write Optimisation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A B-epsilon tree puts buffers of size epsilon B at internal nodes so that inserts are batched before being pushed down, reducing insertion I/Os by a factor B^epsilon.
short: Buffer writes to amortise disk transfers.
long: Buffer writes to amortise disk transfers. Point queries must check buffers along the search path, increasing read cost relative to a B-tree.
proof: Each buffer flush sends epsilon B entries in one I/O, amortising the transfer across many inserts.
consequence: It is a write-optimised index for update-heavy workloads.

title: Buffer Tree for Batched Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A buffer tree attaches an I/O-sized buffer to each node of a B-tree so that batches of updates are pushed down in sorted order.
short: Sort inside the tree to avoid random I/O.
long: Sort inside the tree to avoid random I/O. It is a core technique in cache-oblivious and external-memory graph algorithms.
proof: When a buffer fills, its contents are sorted and distributed in one sequential scan of children.
consequence: Batched updates become dramatically cheaper on disk.

title: R-Tree Spatial Index
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An R-tree indexes spatial objects by enclosing them in minimum bounding rectangles arranged in a balanced tree.
short: Bounding boxes organise objects by location.
long: Bounding boxes organise objects by location. Overlapping rectangles can force a query to visit many branches, so worst-case query time is O(n).
proof: Each internal node groups nearby rectangles, and a window query descends only into overlapping boxes.
consequence: R-trees are the default spatial index in geographic databases.

title: Bounding Volume Hierarchy
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A BVH recursively groups geometric objects into bounding volumes so ray intersection tests prune most of the scene.
short: Skip whole subtrees whose bounding volume misses the ray.
long: Skip whole subtrees whose bounding volume misses the ray. Quality depends on how tightly volumes bound their children and on split heuristics.
proof: A ray must intersect a node's volume before descending into its children.
consequence: BVHs are fundamental to ray tracing and collision detection.

title: Misra-Gries Heavy Hitters Summary
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Keeping k-1 counters and decrementing all on a miss identifies every item with frequency exceeding n/k in one pass with O(k) space.
short: Repeated cancellation preserves frequent items.
long: Repeated cancellation preserves frequent items. Estimated counts may overestimate true counts but never underestimate them.
proof: Each decrement removes k distinct items, so a true heavy hitter cannot be eliminated completely.
consequence: It is the classic streaming heavy-hitters algorithm.

title: Count-Min Sketch Point Estimates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A count-min sketch uses d hash functions into arrays of width w and reports the minimum of the d counters, never underestimating a frequency.
short: Hash collisions only inflate estimates.
long: Hash collisions only inflate estimates. Setting w = O(1/epsilon) and d = O(log(1/delta)) gives the standard guarantee.
proof: Collisions with the queried item are bounded by Markov's inequality and independent across rows.
consequence: It estimates frequencies in small space for streams and networking.

title: HyperLogLog Cardinality Estimation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct stream elements from the maximum number of leading zeros in hashed values across m registers.
short: Rare long runs of zeros reveal the cardinality.
long: Rare long runs of zeros reveal the cardinality. Space is O(m) registers, and a harmonic-mean correction removes bias.
proof: The probability that an item hashes to a value with k leading zeros is 2^{-k}, so the observed maximum estimates log n.
consequence: It estimates huge cardinalities with kilobytes of memory.

title: Quotient Filter Space Efficiency
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A quotient filter stores fingerprints in a hash-table-like array using quotienting, storing only the remainder bits and using the quotient as the bucket address.
short: Hash value doubles as the bucket address.
long: Hash value doubles as the bucket address. It supports insertions, lookups and deletions with locality better than a Bloom filter.
proof: Writing a fingerprint as quotient plus remainder lets the quotient be implicit in its array position.
consequence: It is a compact alternative to Bloom filters for large approximate sets.

title: Cuckoo Filter with Fingerprints
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A cuckoo filter stores short fingerprints in two candidate buckets derived from the key, supporting O(1) lookups and deletions with a small false positive rate.
short: Cuckoo hashing without storing full keys.
long: Cuckoo hashing without storing full keys. False positives arise from fingerprint collisions, so longer fingerprints reduce them at extra space cost.
proof: The two candidate buckets are computed from the key hash and its XOR with the fingerprint hash.
consequence: It gives a deletable, cache-friendly approximate membership structure.

title: Succinct Balanced-Parentheses Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An ordered rooted tree can be encoded in 2n + o(n) bits as a balanced-parentheses sequence supporting navigation in O(1) time.
short: Tree shape needs only two bits per node.
long: Tree shape needs only two bits per node. Rank and select on the bitstring implement parent, child and subtree-size queries.
proof: An open parenthesis denotes descent to a child and a close parenthesis denotes return to the parent.
consequence: Succinct trees compress large XML, DOM and ontology structures without losing access speed.

title: Succinct Graph Representation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A dense undirected graph on n vertices can be stored in n^2 + o(n^2) bits while supporting degree and neighbour queries in constant time.
short: Store the adjacency matrix as bits plus a small index.
long: Store the adjacency matrix as bits plus a small index. Sparse graphs admit o(n^2) bit representations using degree-sorted adjacency lists.
proof: One bit per ordered pair encodes adjacency, and rank/select tables support neighbour enumeration.
consequence: Succinct graph encoding allows large graphs to reside in main memory.

title: Fusion Tree Word-RAM Searching
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A fusion tree searches n w-bit keys in O(log_w n) time by comparing several key bits in one word operation.
short: Pack a whole B-tree node's branching into a word.
long: Pack a whole B-tree node's branching into a word. With w >= log n this improves on the log n comparison bound, at the cost of complex bit manipulation.
proof: Sketching keys to O(log n) significant bits and using a fusion node finds the predecessor among up to w keys in constant time.
consequence: It shows how word-level parallelism breaks comparison-model lower bounds.

title: SWAR Broadword Parallelism
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: SWAR (SIMD within a register) packs several small fields into one machine word so that a single instruction updates all of them.
short: Arithmetic on subwords gives free parallelism.
long: Arithmetic on subwords gives free parallelism. Careful masks prevent carries from crossing field boundaries.
proof: Bitwise AND with repeated masks isolates each field, and one addition updates all fields simultaneously.
consequence: It accelerates bitvectors, succinct structures and small-integer arrays.

title: Retroactive Data Structures
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A retroactive data structure supports updates in the past and queries at arbitrary historical times, rather than only appending new versions.
short: Edit history, not just append to it.
long: Edit history, not just append to it. Partially retroactive structures only allow past updates, while fully retroactive ones also allow past queries.
proof: Operations are stored in a timeline structure and local rebuilding repairs invariants around the modified point.
consequence: They model time-travel debugging and historical database queries.

title: Persistent Array by Path Copying
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A balanced array with path copying supports read and write on any past version in O(log n) time and space.
short: A trie-like tree of chunks lets versions share unchanged blocks.
long: A trie-like tree of chunks lets versions share unchanged blocks. Chunk size is chosen to balance tree depth against copying cost.
proof: A write replaces only the leaf chunk and the log n nodes on its path, leaving all other chunks shared.
consequence: It generalises persistent stacks to random-access arrays.

title: PRAM Shared-Memory Parallel Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: The PRAM model has p synchronous processors sharing a common memory, running in lockstep with unit-time arithmetic and memory operations.
short: An idealised shared-memory parallel computer.
long: An idealised shared-memory parallel computer. Variants differ in whether concurrent reads or writes are allowed; analyse by work and depth.
proof: The model is an abstraction: each processor executes one instruction per step on its local data or shared memory.
consequence: It gives a clean setting for designing parallel algorithms before mapping to real hardware.

title: PRAM Concurrency Variants
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: EREW forbids concurrent reads and writes, CREW allows concurrent reads, and CRCW additionally allows concurrent writes resolved by common, arbitrary or priority rules.
short: Concurrency rules define the machine's power.
long: Concurrency rules define the machine's power. Algorithms designed for EREW are portable; CRCW can be more powerful for tasks such as leader election.
proof: Each model is a restriction or extension of the previous one's permitted memory-access patterns.
consequence: State the assumed variant when quoting PRAM running times.

title: Parallel Prefix Scan
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: An associative parallel prefix computes all running aggregates of n values in O(log n) depth and O(n) work.
short: Up-sweep and down-sweep compute all prefixes at once.
long: Up-sweep and down-sweep compute all prefixes at once. Scan is the parallel analogue of prefix sums and underlies sorting, compaction and recurrence solvers.
proof: A balanced reduction tree computes partial aggregates; a downward pass distributes carried prefixes to siblings.
consequence: Work-efficient scans are a core primitive of parallel algorithms.

title: Parallel Reduce and Map Patterns
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Map applies a function independently to all inputs and reduce combines them with an associative operator, giving O(log n) depth with O(n) work.
short: Independent mapping plus a reduction tree.
long: Independent mapping plus a reduction tree. These patterns are the building blocks of GPU and data-parallel frameworks.
proof: Mapping is embarrassingly parallel and reduction is a binary tree of associative operations.
consequence: They express many algorithms without explicit synchronisation.

title: Cole's Parallel Merge Sort Depth
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Cole's parallel merge sort sorts n keys on an EREW PRAM in O(log n) time using O(n log n) work.
short: Pipelining merges removes a logarithmic factor from depth.
long: Pipelining merges removes a logarithmic factor from depth. Naive parallel merge sort has O(log^2 n) depth; Cole's chained decomposition improves it.
proof: Dividing merges into small pipelined blocks allows each level to start before the previous one finishes while keeping work linearithmic.
consequence: It shows comparison sorting has logarithmic parallel depth with near-optimal work.

title: Parallel BFS Frontier Expansion
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Breadth-first search can process each layer in parallel by relaxing all outgoing edges of the current frontier, taking O(D) depth and O(V+E) work.
short: All vertices in a layer expand simultaneously.
long: All vertices in a layer expand simultaneously. Duplicate discoveries must be resolved atomically; low-diameter graphs expose the most parallelism.
proof: Layers are independent because edges within a layer cannot shorten distances to the next layer in an unweighted graph.
consequence: It is the standard parallel graph-traversal primitive.

title: MapReduce Programming Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: MapReduce processes data with a map function producing key-value pairs, a shuffle that groups pairs by key, and a reduce function aggregating each group.
short: Group by key, then aggregate.
long: Group by key, then aggregate. The framework handles parallelism, fault tolerance and data distribution.
proof: All records with the same key are routed to the same reducer, so reductions are independent.
consequence: It made large-scale batch data processing accessible to ordinary programmers.

title: MapReduce Sorting with Range Partitioners
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sampling the key distribution to choose partition boundaries lets MapReduce sort records with balanced reducer loads and local sorting at each reducer.
short: Partition by sampled ranges, then sort locally.
long: Partition by sampled ranges, then sort locally. Each reducer receives a contiguous key range, so concatenating reducer outputs yields a globally sorted file.
proof: Sample-based quantiles approximate equal-sized partitions, and local sorting preserves order within each range.
consequence: It is how production systems sort datasets far larger than one machine's memory.

title: MapReduce Join by Key
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A equi-join of two datasets can be implemented by mapping each record to its join key and reducing over the grouped pairs.
short: Matching keys meet at the same reducer.
long: Matching keys meet at the same reducer. Skew in key frequencies can overload one reducer, requiring skew-handling techniques.
proof: Every output pair agrees on its key, and all such pairs are co-located by the shuffle.
consequence: It is a fundamental large-scale database primitive.

title: Bulk Synchronous Parallel Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: BSP computes in supersteps: local computation, message sending, then a global barrier before the next superstep.
short: Compute, communicate, synchronise, repeat.
long: Compute, communicate, synchronise, repeat. Parameters are computation cost w, communication cost h times network gap g, and synchronization period L.
proof: The model charges each superstep for its slowest processor plus communication and barrier costs.
consequence: It gives predictable performance on distributed-memory machines.
